steps.text: Legs apart and bent, weight low, shoulders forward. The pelvis drops: that is what gives the feeling of stability.

steps.title: Sitting, relaxed
steps.text: The weight rests on the pelvis, not on the legs. Let the back round, the head tilt, and one leg do something different from the other.

tips: Draw fast: the shorter the sketch, the more alive the gesture. Aim for 30 to 60 seconds per pose.
Strike the pose yourself in a mirror or a selfie: you'll feel where your weight goes.
Start with the leg carrying the weight: the rest of the body organizes itself around it.
Stiff pose? Tilt the head, shift the shoulders and bend a knee. That is often enough.
Hair and clothes extend the movement: make them follow the line of action.
Before drawing a character in the app, look for their line of action: you'll see why the pose works.
topics.practice: Do 10 sketches of 30 seconds from photos. Pick your favorite and rebuild it with the four steps of this lesson.

topics.title: Hair
topics.summary: A helmet, a few locks, and movement.
topics.intro: Hair often makes a manga character's whole silhouette: you recognize them by their hairstyle before you even see their face. The secret is to think of hair as masses before thinking of it as locks.

chapters.title: Building a hairstyle in four steps

steps.title: The skull first
steps.text: Draw the whole head, skull included, even if it will be hidden. Hair goes on top of it: it doesn't replace the top of the head.

steps.title: The volume
steps.text: Draw a helmet a little bigger than the skull, a finger or two above it. Hair stuck to the skull makes the head look too small.

steps.title: Hairline and parting
steps.text: Mark where the hair starts on the forehead, and the parting if the character has one. Every lock starts from there.

steps.title: The big locks
steps.text: Cut the helmet into a few big locks that start at the parting or the crown and follow the curve of the head. Small locks come last.

chapters.callout: If the hairstyle looks flat, check the top of the skull: it almost always lacks volume at the crown.

chapters.title: Drawing a lock
bullets: A lock is a ribbon, not a line: two strokes that start together and meet in a point.
Vary their size: a few big ones, some medium ones and two or three small ones. Locks that are all alike look like a saw blade.
Overlap them: a lock passing in front of another creates depth right away.
Keep the tips going in the same general direction, then let one or two locks escape. That bit of mess makes the hair look natural.
Don't draw every hair: a few thin strokes inside the big locks are enough to give texture.

steps.title: Short and spiky
steps.text: The shonen hero's hairstyle: big pointed locks leaving the crown in every direction. Keep an overall fan shape.

steps.title: Bob and bangs
steps.text: The mass falls straight and stops at the jaw. The bangs follow the curve of the forehead, with tips of different lengths.

steps.title: Long
steps.text: The hair falls past the shoulders in a few long locks that widen, then thin out. Always separate what falls in front of the shoulder from what falls behind it.

steps.title: Tied up
steps.text: For a ponytail, the hair is pulled toward the hair tie: every lock converges on it, tight against the skull. The volume opens up again after it.

chapters.title: Hair in motion
chapters.intro: Moving hair brings a panel to life, even when the character stands still.

steps.title: Find the force
steps.text: Wind, a turn of the head or a run: decide where the force comes from. Every lock points the other way.

steps.title: Keep the roots
steps.text: The hair stays fixed to the skull: only the tips fly. The longer a lock, the more it moves.

steps.title: Behind the movement
steps.text: When the head turns, the hair follows a moment later. Draw it still on the side the movement comes from.

steps.title: S curves
steps.text: A floating lock waves in an S and thins toward its tip. A straight line looks stiff, like plastic.

chapters.callout: Make the clothes move the same way as the hair: if they disagree, the eye feels something is off.

tips: Draw the hair once the face is in place: it is built on the head, not the other way around.
Mass first, locks next, single hairs never.
For shine, leave a white band following the curve of the skull, with a zigzag edge.
A hairstyle is recognized by its silhouette: fill it in black, and if it still reads, it works.
In the app, trace a hairstyle you like and find its parting: you'll see where every lock starts.
topics.practice: Draw the same head three times and give it a different hairstyle each time: short and spiky, bob with bangs, long. Always start with the helmet.

topics.title: Chibi
topics.summary: A character two to three heads tall.
topics.intro: A chibi is a pocket-sized version of a character, with a big head and a small body. It is used for comic scenes, stickers and merch. It is also a great exercise: it forces you to keep only what matters in a character.

chapters.title: The proportions

steps.title: Count in heads
steps.text: An adult manga character is about 7 heads tall. A chibi is only 2 to 3: the head alone makes a third to a half of the height.

steps.title: The head
steps.text: A big sphere with a short, rounded chin. The eyes move below the middle of the head and become very big.

steps.title: The body
steps.text: A small bean- or pear-shaped torso, about half as tall as the head. No waist, no muscles.

steps.title: The limbs
steps.text: Short, rounded arms and legs, with no visible elbows or knees. Hands become mittens, feet small ovals.

chapters.callout: If your chibi looks like a child rather than a chibi, the head isn't big enough: make it bigger before touching anything else.

chapters.title: Simplifying the face
bullets: The nose disappears or becomes a tiny dot.
The mouth is a small line or shape, placed very low, close to the chin.
The eyes take up almost the whole width of the face, with big highlights.
The ears are small or hidden by the hair.
The hair keeps the overall shape of the character's hairstyle, but with fewer, bigger locks.

chapters.title: Turning a character into a chibi

steps.title: Find what makes them unique
steps.text: Their hairstyle, their outfit, an accessory, their main color. These are what must stay.

steps.title: Keep, enlarge, remove
steps.text: Enlarge what matters (an iconic lock, a weapon, a hat) and remove the small details (folds, buttons, patterns).

steps.title: A pose that tells who they are
steps.text: A chibi shows its personality through its pose: arms up for an energetic character, hands behind the back for a shy one.

chapters.title: Chibis in action
chapters.intro: With such a short body, every movement has to be exaggerated to read.

steps.title: The line of action
steps.text: It matters even more than on a regular character: bend the whole body in one direction, from head to feet.

steps.title: The head leads
steps.text: Tilt the big head toward the movement: it shows the direction far more than the little arms.

steps.title: Stretchy limbs
steps.text: To run or punch, stretch an arm or a leg a bit longer than usual. On a chibi, nobody will call it cheating.

steps.title: The effects around
steps.text: Speed lines, little dust clouds, stars: on a chibi, they do half of the action.

chapters.callout: Keep both feet firmly planted when the chibi stands still: with such a heavy head, it has to look stable.

tips: Always build the head first and the body under it: the head sets the scale.
Thicker, rounder lines make a chibi cuter: avoid sharp angles.
Try several head sizes side by side: 2 heads for a very cute style, 3 for a more readable one.
Chibi expressions can be very simple: a line for closed eyes, an oval for surprise.
Pick a character from the catalog you have already drawn and make their chibi version: you already know their details.
topics.practice: Pick a character you like and draw them at three sizes: 3 heads, 2.5 heads and 2 heads. Keep their hairstyle and outfit recognizable each time.

topics.title: Perspective
topics.summary: Horizon, vanishing points and characters in a scene.
topics.intro: Perspective is what keeps a character standing in a scene: without it, they float. You don't need complicated rules to start: a horizon line and one or two points are enough to make a scene believable.

chapters.title: The horizon line

steps.title: It's your eye level
steps.text: The horizon line is always at the viewer's eye level, whether or not the real line between sky and ground can be seen.

steps.title: Above or below
steps.text: What is below the horizon is seen from above; what is above it is seen from below. A table shows its top, a ceiling shows its underside.

steps.title: One height, one feeling
steps.text: Low horizon: the scene feels big and imposing. High horizon: we look down on the scene and the characters feel small.

steps.title: Draw it first
steps.text: Before even the first character, place the horizon. Everything else in the panel is organized around it.

chapters.callout: One horizon per panel. Two horizons mean two cameras, and the eye feels that the scene is broken.

chapters.title: One and two vanishing points

steps.title: One vanishing point
steps.text: Put a point on the horizon. Every line going into the depth converges toward it: a corridor, a road, rails. Perfect for a scene seen from the front.

steps.title: Two vanishing points
steps.text: Put two points far apart on the horizon. Each side of a box runs toward one of them, and verticals stay vertical. It is the three-quarter view of a building.

steps.title: Points far from the drawing
steps.text: Vanishing points too close together warp everything. Don't hesitate to put them outside the sheet.

chapters.callout: The boxes of week 2 of the program are exactly this: every box you drew had its vanishing points.

chapters.title: Placing characters in a scene

steps.title: The horizon crosses everyone at the same place
steps.text: If the camera is at a person's height, the horizon goes through the eyes of every standing character, near or far. Only their size changes.

steps.title: Farther, higher and smaller
steps.text: A character farther away has their feet higher on the page, closer to the horizon, and is smaller.

steps.title: Feet on the ground
steps.text: Draw the ground around the feet, even roughly: a shadow or a line is enough to keep a character from floating.

chapters.callout: A seated or shorter character doesn't have their eyes on the horizon: measure them against a standing character next to them.

chapters.title: High and low angles
chapters.intro: When the camera looks up or down, verticals are no longer parallel: they run to a third point. It is the angle of fights and towering heroes.

steps.title: The third point
steps.text: Put it far above the panel for a low angle, far below it for a high angle. The verticals of buildings and bodies converge on it.

steps.title: Low angle: power
steps.text: Seen from below, the feet are big, the head small, the chin and the underside of the nose visible. The character towers over the reader.

steps.title: High angle: vulnerability
steps.text: Seen from above, the head and shoulders are big and the legs get shorter. We see the top of the skull and the ground around the character.

steps.title: Build with boxes
steps.text: First draw the rib cage and pelvis as boxes in this perspective: the rest of the body follows.

chapters.callout: Keep these angles for big moments: if they are everywhere, they stop surprising.

tips: Take a photo of your room and trace the floor and ceiling lines over it: you'll see where the vanishing points are.
Use a ruler for perspective lines at first: freehand will come later.
You don't need a full background: a floor, a wall and a door are enough to set a scene.
If something looks off, extend its lines: the one that doesn't go to the right point is the culprit.
In the app, look at characters seen from above or below and find where their verticals would go.
topics.practice: Draw a horizon and two vanishing points, then a street with three boxes for buildings and three standing characters at different distances, their eyes on the horizon.

topics.title: Light and shadow
topics.summary: One light source, two shadows, and volume appears.
topics.intro: A line drawing shows a shape; light gives it volume. You only need one rule, where the light comes from, to place every shadow on a character without hesitating.

chapters.title: A single light source

steps.title: Decide where it comes from
steps.text: Before the first shadow, choose where the light comes from: top left, for example. Mark it with a small arrow in a corner.

steps.title: What faces it is lit
steps.text: Surfaces turned toward the light stay light. Those turning away from it go into shadow.

steps.title: The border follows the form
steps.text: The border between light and shadow hugs the volume: curved on a sphere, straight on a box, a band on a cylinder.

steps.title: Test on simple volumes
steps.text: Before a character, shade a sphere, a box and a cylinder with the same light. A body is just these shapes put together.

chapters.callout: A shadow that switches sides from one object to the next means two lights: the drawing instantly loses credibility.

chapters.title: Form shadow and cast shadow
bullets: The form shadow is on the object itself: the side that doesn't see the light.
The cast shadow is the one the object throws onto something else: the ground, a wall, another character.
The cast shadow starts at the object, on the side away from the light. The lower the light, the longer it gets.
On a character, the most useful cast shadows: the head on the neck, the bangs on the forehead, the arm on the torso, the nose on the cheek.
A cast shadow under the feet is enough to put a character on the ground.

steps.title: A single shadow tone
steps.text: Anime often uses a single shadow tone with a crisp edge. No gradient: the shape of the shadow is enough to show the volume.

steps.title: Simple shapes
steps.text: Draw the shadow as a graphic shape: a crescent on the cheek, a triangle under the nose, a band under the chin.

steps.title: Folds and hollows
steps.text: Add shadows in the hollows: under the bangs, in the folds of the clothes, under the arms. Light never reaches these places.

steps.title: A highlight if needed
steps.text: To finish, a small light spot on the hair or the eyes makes them shine.

chapters.title: Backlight and mood lighting
chapters.intro: Changing the light changes the mood of a panel without touching the drawing.

steps.title: Backlight
steps.text: The light comes from behind: the character is almost all in shadow, and only a thin bright rim outlines them. Perfect for a mysterious entrance.

steps.title: Light from below
steps.text: Light coming from below, like a flashlight, flips the shadows of the face. A sure effect for a menacing character.

steps.title: Two lights
steps.text: A strong main light and a weaker one on the other side, in another color: the scene gains depth. Always keep one dominant light.

steps.title: Night
steps.text: Darken the whole drawing, then add the lights: a window, a street lamp, a phone screen. They are what guides the eye.

chapters.callout: The stronger the contrast between light and shadow, the more dramatic the scene. Soft lighting suits calm moments.

tips: Light a simple object with your phone's flashlight in a dark room and move the light around: you'll see the shadows move.
Squint at a reference: details disappear and only the big masses of light and shadow remain.
A few well-placed shadows beat many shadows everywhere.
Keep the face mostly in the light: that's where the reader looks.
In the app, pick a character and guess where the light would come from, based on their shadows, before tracing them.
topics.practice: Draw a sphere, a box and a cylinder side by side. Pick a light at the top left and give each one its form shadow and its cast shadow, in a single tone.

topics.title: Inking
topics.summary: Confident lines, and line weight that builds volume.
topics.intro: Inking turns a sketch into a finished drawing. It isn't going over the pencil: it's choosing the right line, drawing it in one stroke, and using its thickness to add depth.

chapters.title: A confident line

steps.title: Draw with your arm
steps.text: For a long curve, move from the elbow or the shoulder, not the wrist. The wrist makes short, shaky strokes.

steps.title: Ghost the motion
steps.text: Before putting the pen down, do the motion two or three times just above the paper. Then draw it in one go.

steps.title: One line, not ten
steps.text: A line made of small overlapping strokes looks hesitant. Better a confident line that's slightly off.

steps.title: Turn the page
steps.text: Your hand has easy directions. Turn the paper, or the canvas on a tablet, so you always draw in the direction that suits you.

chapters.callout: On a tablet, stroke stabilization helps, but it doesn't replace the gesture: practice without it too.

chapters.title: Varying line weight
bullets: A character's outer contour is thicker than the inner lines: it separates them from the background.
Lines on the shadow side are thicker, lines on the light side thinner, or even broken.
What is close to the reader gets a thicker line than what is far.
Thicken the line where two forms cross or overlap: under the chin, under locks of hair, in folds.
Taper lines at their ends: a tapering line looks alive, a line of even width looks mechanical.

chapters.title: Hatching

steps.title: Parallel lines
steps.text: Short lines, all in the same direction, evenly spaced. The tighter they are, the darker the area.

steps.title: Cross-hatching
steps.text: Add a second layer in another direction for the deepest shadows.

steps.title: Follow the form
steps.text: Curve the hatching around the volume, like lines hugging the surface: they describe the form as well as the shadow.

chapters.callout: In manga, hatching is mostly for shadows on faces and hair and for tense moods. Use it sparingly.

chapters.title: Inking a whole illustration
chapters.intro: Inking a whole drawing takes method: the order you work in changes the result.

steps.title: Clean pencils
steps.text: Clean your sketch up into neater pencils, in light blue or on a faded layer. The ink shouldn't be searching for the shape anymore.

steps.title: From the most important to the details
steps.text: Start with the face, then the body's contours, then the clothes, and finish with the hair and small details.

steps.title: Big blacks at the end
steps.text: Fill the blacks (hair, dark clothes, deep shadows) once every line is down. They balance the page.

steps.title: Go over the contour
steps.text: To finish, thicken the character's outer contour. That last pass makes them pop.

chapters.callout: Let the ink dry before erasing the pencil, or hide the sketch layer on a tablet, to judge the drawing on its own.

tips: Warm up for two minutes with lines and circles before inking: the first line of the day is always the shakiest.
A fine 0.3 mm felt-tip pen and a thicker 0.8 mm one are enough to start.
Draw fast: a slow line wobbles, a fast line flows.
Don't go over a missed line: keep going, and fix it on the next drawing.
In the app, trace a character using only single-stroke lines, without going over them.
topics.practice: Fill a page with long curves, each drawn in a single stroke, then ink one of your sketches, thickening the outer contour and the shadow side.

topics.title: Feet
topics.summary: A wedge, a heel, and the character stands.
topics.intro: After hands, feet are what we hide most, often behind the framing or a vague shoe. Yet the whole weight of the character rests on them. Well built, they keep the character on the ground.

chapters.title: Building a foot in four steps

steps.title: A wedge
steps.text: Seen from the side, the foot is a wedge: high at the ankle, sloping down to the toes. Start with this simple shape.

steps.title: The heel
steps.text: Add a ball under and behind the ankle. The heel sticks out to the back: without it, the character tips over.

steps.title: The arch
steps.text: On the inner side, the foot doesn't touch the ground in the middle: carve an arch between the heel and the ball of the foot. On the outer side, it stays almost flat.

steps.title: Toes as a block
steps.text: First draw the toes as one rounded block, then separate the big toe from the other four. They step down toward the outside.

chapters.callout: A foot is about as long as the head is tall. If it looks too small, the character seems unstable.

chapters.title: Landmarks to remember
bullets: The inner ankle bone is higher than the outer one.
Seen from the front, the foot widens toward the toes: narrow at the heel, wide at the front.
The big toe is separated from the others by a small gap and points straight ahead.
From the front, you mostly see the top of the foot and shortened toes: the heel disappears behind.
When the character walks, the back foot bends at the toes, heel lifted.

steps.title: From the side
steps.text: The easiest view: the wedge, the heel, the arch. Always start with it to understand a foot.

steps.title: From the front
steps.text: A trapezoid widening toward the bottom, the toes in a fan, the ankle above. The nearest toes partly hide the top of the foot.

steps.title: Three-quarter view
steps.text: A mix of both: you see the arch on one side and the top of the foot. Keep the heel visible, even slightly.

chapters.title: Shoes
chapters.intro: A shoe is drawn like clothing: around the foot, never instead of it.

steps.title: The foot first
steps.text: Draw the foot, even roughly, then the shoe over it, a little bigger. The shape of the foot must stay readable underneath.

steps.title: The sole
steps.text: Draw the sole as a flat box under the foot, following the curve of the arch. The thicker it is, the heavier the shoe looks.

steps.title: The sneaker
steps.text: A rounded toe, laces following the curve of the top of the foot, a padded collar around the ankle.

steps.title: The boot
steps.text: The foot plus a cylinder for the shaft, running up the calf. Add a few folds at the ankle, where it bends.

chapters.callout: A shoe creases where the foot bends: above the toes and at the ankle.

tips: Your own feet are free models: draw them from several angles, with and without shoes.
Always draw a ground line under the feet: you'll see right away if the character stands.
The foot carrying the weight is flat; the other one can lift, turn or rest on its toes.
Don't draw both feet exactly alike and parallel: they point slightly outward.
In the app, pick full-body characters and look at how their shoes follow the shape of the foot.
topics.practice: Draw five feet as wedges from different angles, add the heel, the arch and the toes, then finish with a pair of feet from the front, standing on a ground line.

topics.title: The manga page
topics.intro: A page is a drawing that tells a story over time. The reader must know where to look and in what order, without ever wondering. A few simple rules are enough to get there.

chapters.title: Laying out a page

steps.title: Reading order
steps.text: A Japanese manga reads right to left and top to bottom: you start with the top-right panel. Choose a direction and keep it for your whole story.

steps.title: Horizontal tiers
steps.text: Split the page into 3 to 5 tiers, then split each tier into panels. The reader finishes a tier before moving on to the next.

steps.title: Size means importance
steps.text: A big panel for a strong moment, small panels for what goes by quickly. A page of equal panels lacks rhythm.

steps.title: Clear gutters
steps.text: Leave a regular gap between panels, wider between tiers than between the panels of a tier. That gap is what guides the reading order.

chapters.callout: Draft your page tiny first, as stamp-sized thumbnails: you see the rhythm far better than at full size.

chapters.title: Balloons
bullets: Place the balloons before drawing: they take up space and must hide neither a face nor an action.
Balloons read in the same order as the panels: the first one at the top right, or the top left, depending on your reading direction.
The balloon's tail points toward the speaker's mouth, without touching it.
A round balloon to speak, a cloud to think, a spiky one to shout.
Little text per balloon: if one overflows, split it in two.

steps.title: A wide shot to set the scene
steps.text: Open a scene with a wide panel that shows where we are and who is there. Only then move closer.

steps.title: The 180-degree rule
steps.text: If a character faces left in one panel, keep them on the left in the next while they talk to the same person. Otherwise the reader gets lost.

steps.title: The last panel
steps.text: The panel at the bottom of the page makes the reader want to turn it: a question, a surprise, a look.

chapters.title: Rhythm and action panels
chapters.intro: In an action scene, the layout itself becomes an effect: it speeds time up or slows it down.

steps.title: Slanted panels
steps.text: Slanted borders add tension and speed. Keep them for action: in a calm scene, they are tiring.

steps.title: Breaking out of the panel
steps.text: Let a fist, a sword or a character spill over into the next panel: the action seems to burst out of the page.

steps.title: Slowing time down
steps.text: Several small panels on the same instant (a look, a hand, a drop of sweat) stretch the moment just before the impact.

steps.title: The full page
steps.text: Save a panel that takes the whole page, or a double spread, for the strongest moment of the chapter. One per chapter, no more.

chapters.callout: A panel that bleeds to the edge of the page feels bigger and more immersive than its real size.

tips: Take a page from your favorite manga and trace only its panels: you'll see its skeleton.
Write the balloon text before drawing: it often decides the size of the panels.
Alternate shots: wide, medium, close-up. Three panels in a row with the same framing feel frozen.
Avoid panels that could be read in two orders: if you hesitate, the reader will too.
Put characters from the app's catalog in a little four-panel story: it's the best exercise to start with.
topics.practice: Make a yonkoma, a story in four vertical panels: a setup, a development, a twist and a punchline. Keep it simple, stick figures are fine.

topics.title: Composition and framing
topics.summary: Where to place the subject and how to frame it.
topics.intro: The same drawing can be dull or striking depending on where it sits in the frame. Composition is the art of guiding the reader's eye to what matters.

chapters.title: The rule of thirds

steps.title: A grid of nine
steps.text: Mentally split your frame into three, in width and in height. You get four lines and four crossing points.

steps.title: The subject on a strong point
steps.text: Put the face or the important element on one of the four points rather than in the center. The image breathes and feels more alive.

steps.title: The horizon on a third
steps.text: Put the horizon line on the top or bottom third, never in the middle: otherwise the frame looks cut in half.

steps.title: Room in front of the gaze
steps.text: Leave more room on the side the character looks or moves toward. Pressed against the edge they face, they seem stuck.

chapters.callout: The center isn't forbidden: it makes a stable, solemn or face-to-face image. Choose it on purpose, not by default.

chapters.title: Shot sizes
bullets: Wide shot: the whole setting, the characters small. To set a scene.
Full shot: the whole character, head to toe. To show a pose or an action.
Medium shot: from the head to the waist. The dialogue shot.
Close-up: the face. For an emotion.
Extreme close-up: an eye, a hand, a detail. For a moment of tension.

chapters.title: Guiding the eye

steps.title: Contrast attracts
steps.text: The eye goes first to where the contrast is strongest: a light face on a dark background, a black spot in a light setting.

steps.title: Lines that point
steps.text: Background lines, an outstretched arm, a gaze: everything that points leads the eye. Make them converge on your subject.

steps.title: Less detail around
steps.text: Keep the detail on the subject and simplify the rest. A busy background steals the attention.

chapters.callout: Squint at your drawing: what you see first is what the reader will see first.

chapters.title: Studying a pro's panel
chapters.intro: Mangaka learn by taking apart other artists' work. A pro's panel is a free composition lesson.

steps.title: Find the subject
steps.text: What does the panel want to show? A face, a gesture, a place? Write it down in one word.

steps.title: Trace the structure
steps.text: On a layer or a copy, trace the horizon, the main lines and the grid of thirds in a few strokes. See where the subject falls.

steps.title: Find the values
steps.text: Fill the big areas in three tones: white, gray, black. You'll see how the contrast leads the eye.

steps.title: Redo it differently
steps.text: Redraw the panel changing a single thing: the shot, the angle or where the subject sits. Compare what you lose and what you gain.

chapters.callout: Do it with the panels that stay with you: they have the most to teach you.

tips: Make three small thumbnails before each illustration, with three different compositions, and keep the best one.
Flip your drawing horizontally: an unbalanced composition jumps out.
When a character is cut by the edge of the frame, cut between two joints, mid-thigh or mid-arm, never right at the knee or the wrist.
Avoid tangents: two contours that just barely touch are confusing. Overlap them clearly or move them apart.
Before tracing a character in the app, decide on its final framing: full shot, medium shot or close-up.
topics.practice: Draw the same character in three frames of the same size: a wide shot, a medium shot and a close-up, placing their face on a third's point each time.

topics.title: Black, white and screentones
topics.summary: Solid blacks, screentones and black-and-white readability.
topics.intro: Manga is read in black and white: without color, solid blacks and screentones separate the shapes, create the shadows and set the mood. Well balanced, they give a page its impact.

chapters.title: Solid blacks

steps.title: Choose what is black
steps.text: Dark hair, dark clothes, deep shadows: decide at the pencil stage which areas will be black.

steps.title: Balance the page
steps.text: Spread the blacks over the whole page rather than bunching them in a corner. The eye travels from one to the next.

steps.title: Black makes things stand out
steps.text: A light character in front of a black background, or the reverse, reads instantly. Avoid gray on gray.

steps.title: Keep highlights
steps.text: Leave a few white lines in big blacks, on hair or a leather garment: the black keeps its volume.

chapters.callout: A page without any black looks bland; a page with too much becomes unreadable. Aim for a balance of white, gray and black.

chapters.title: Screentones
bullets: A screentone is a pattern of dots that makes a gray. The bigger or tighter the dots, the darker the gray.
Use few different grays: two or three values are enough for a whole page.
A light tone for skin in shadow or colored clothes, a darker one for shadows and backgrounds.
A gradient tone for a sky, falling light or an emotional background.
On a tablet, drawing apps have ready-made tones; on paper, hatching does the same job.

steps.title: Focus lines
steps.text: Lines converging on the character: surprise, revelation, shock.

steps.title: Flowers and bubbles
steps.text: A background of flowers, bubbles or sparkles: a romantic moment or a dazzling character.

steps.title: Black and vertical lines
steps.text: A black background, or one striped with vertical lines: despair, threat, unease.

chapters.title: Moods: night, rain and memories
chapters.intro: Tones aren't only for shading: they change the time and place of a scene without a word.

steps.title: Night
steps.text: A dark tone over the whole sky and the backgrounds, the character left light where a light falls on them. Bold solid blacks for the shadows.

steps.title: Rain
steps.text: Thin white lines scratched diagonally over a gray tone, all in the same direction. Add splashes on the ground.

steps.title: A memory
steps.text: Panels with blurred or rounded edges, a black background around the panels, or a soft light tone over the whole scene.

steps.title: Tension
steps.text: Backgrounds getting darker from one panel to the next: the page darkens with the situation.

chapters.callout: Keep the same mood from panel to panel within a scene: a change of tone tells the reader the moment has changed.

tips: Squint at your page: if everything turns gray, add blacks.
Test your blacks on a copy of the drawing before touching the original.
Don't tone everything: the white areas matter as much as the gray ones.
Look at a manga page from a distance: you'll see its big black shapes. That's its structure.
In the app, trace a character, then choose their black areas: hair, clothes, shadows.
topics.practice: Take one of your drawings and make three versions of it: line only, with solid blacks, then with blacks and a single gray in hatching or tone.

topics.title: Character design
topics.summary: Creating a character people recognize at first glance.
topics.intro: The most famous characters are recognizable by their silhouette alone. Creating a character isn't piling on details: it's finding a few strong choices that say who they are.

chapters.title: A readable silhouette

steps.title: The black test
steps.text: Fill your character in black. If you still recognize them and understand the pose, the silhouette works.

steps.title: One unique element
steps.text: A hairstyle, a hat, a weapon, a cape: give them at least one shape no other character has.

steps.title: Different shapes in a group
steps.text: In a team, vary the sizes and shapes: a tall one, a short one, a stocky one, a thin one. You can tell them apart even from afar.

steps.title: Open up the shapes
steps.text: Move the arms away from the body, show the profile of the hairstyle: a silhouette where everything sticks together becomes a blob.

chapters.callout: If two of your characters have the same silhouette, change their hairstyle first: it's the fastest way to tell them apart.

chapters.title: Shapes and personality
bullets: Circles feel soft, kind and friendly: perfect for a likable or comic character.
Squares feel solid, reliable and stubborn: for a protector, a strongman, a mentor.
Triangles feel sharp, dangerous and ambitious: for a rival, a villain or an edgy hero.
Mix them: one dominant shape for the personality, another as an accent for nuance.
The shape shows up everywhere: in the hairstyle, the eyes, the clothes, the accessories.

steps.title: Three colors
steps.text: A main color, a secondary one and an accent. More than that, and the character gets hard to remember.

steps.title: Details with a story
steps.text: A scar, a bracelet, an oversized scarf: each detail should say something about their past or their personality.

steps.title: Easy to redraw
steps.text: You'll draw them hundreds of times: keep details you can redraw quickly, and always the same way.

chapters.title: The model sheet
chapters.intro: A model sheet shows the character from several angles, at the same proportions. It keeps them identical from one panel to the next.

steps.title: Guide lines
steps.text: Draw horizontal lines across the whole sheet: top of the skull, eyes, chin, shoulders, waist, knees, feet. Every drawing lines up on them.

steps.title: Front, three-quarter, side, back
steps.text: Draw the character standing, arms slightly apart, from these four angles, side by side.

steps.title: Details on the side
steps.text: Add the important details, enlarged, in a corner: an accessory, a pattern, the shape of the eyes.

steps.title: A few expressions
steps.text: Finish with three or four heads showing their typical expressions.

chapters.callout: Keep the sheet next to you when you draw the character: even pros check it for every panel.

tips: Start with a sentence: who is this character, and what do they want? The drawing comes after.
Make ten quick black silhouettes before choosing: the most original ideas rarely come first.
Exaggerate a personality trait in the drawing: a shy one slightly hunched, a proud one chest out.
Avoid details you don't like drawing: you'll end up forgetting or botching them.
In the app, trace a well-known character, then fill their silhouette in black: see what makes them recognizable.
topics.practice: Draw five black silhouettes of invented characters, each built on a shape: circle, square or triangle. Pick the strongest one and draw it in line.

topics.title: Action effects
topics.intro: In manga, action isn't only in the pose: the effects around the character make you feel speed, force and impact. A few well-placed lines turn a frozen panel into a fight scene.

chapters.title: Speed lines

steps.title: In the direction of the movement
steps.text: Draw parallel lines behind the character, in the direction they come from. They show the path they've just traveled.

steps.title: Tapering lines
steps.text: Each line starts thick near the character and thins out as it goes. Vary their length.

steps.title: A rushing background
steps.text: For extreme speed, fill the whole background with parallel lines: the setting disappears, only the movement remains.

steps.title: Focus lines
steps.text: Lines converging on a point, like the spokes of a wheel: they draw the eye to a face or an attack coming at the reader.

chapters.callout: Leave white space around the character: lines touching their outline make them unreadable.

chapters.title: Impacts
bullets: A star shape with uneven points at the point of contact: the flash of the hit.
Cracks and debris flying from the point of impact, smaller as they get farther.
Small curved strokes around an object that vibrates or shakes.
A cloud of dust under the feet when landing or taking off.
A shockwave in concentric circles for an explosion or a powerful shout.

chapters.title: Squash and stretch

steps.title: Stretch for speed
steps.text: A body or object moving fast stretches in the direction of the movement: a thrown fist looks longer, a jumping character stretches out.

steps.title: Squash on impact
steps.text: At the moment of impact, the shape flattens against what it hits, before getting its shape back.

steps.title: Keep the volume
steps.text: What stretches gets thinner, what squashes gets wider: the total volume stays the same, or the shape seems to swell or melt.

chapters.callout: It's the first of the twelve principles of animation: it works as well in a still panel as in a cartoon.

chapters.title: A fight scene in three panels
chapters.intro: A good fight reads like a sentence: each panel is a word, and the reader must feel the blow before even seeing it.

steps.title: The wind-up
steps.text: First panel: the character winds up, body coiled, eyes locked on the target. Often a close-up on the eyes or a fist clenching.

steps.title: The hit
steps.text: Second panel, the biggest: the movement fully stretched, speed lines, an impact. Pick a strong angle, from below or with the fist toward the reader.

steps.title: The aftermath
steps.text: Third panel: the opponent knocked back, the dust settling, a look. It tells whether the blow landed.

steps.title: Keep the direction
steps.text: If the attack goes from right to left in the first panel, it must keep that direction in the next ones. The reader follows the movement effortlessly.

chapters.callout: The moment just before the impact is often stronger than the impact itself: don't hesitate to give it its own panel.

tips: Draw the character first and the effects after, on a separate layer if you're on a tablet.
Draw speed lines fast, in one stroke: a slow line looks limp.
Fewer, stronger effects: a panel saturated with effects loses its readability.
Hair and clothes must go the same way as the speed lines.
In the app, pick a character in the middle of an action and imagine the effects around them before tracing.
topics.practice: Draw a bouncing ball in five positions, stretched as it falls and squashed on the ground, then a simple character running with speed lines behind them.

w1.title: The head from every angle
w1.text: Build a complete manga head, eyes, nose, mouth, ears and hair, from the front, in three-quarter view and in profile.

w1d1.title: The head as a volume
w1d1.text: A manga head isn't a flat circle: it's a ball you carve. Four steps, always the same.

w1d1-1.title: The head as a volume, Warm-up
w1d1-1.text: Draw 10 quick circles of the same size: they'll be your skulls.

w1d1-2.title: The head as a volume, The method
w1d1-2.text: Every manga head is built in the same 4 steps, whichever way it turns. Follow them in order. The skull: a sphere: A circle for the skull. It's the main volume: everything else hangs on it. The side plane: Cut a slice off the side of the sphere: that's the temple, where the ear will go. The axis of the face: A curved vertical line through the middle of the face. It follows the turn of the head. Jaw and chin: Come down from each side of the skull to the chin. In manga, the chin is thin and a little pointed.

w1d1-3.title: The head as a volume, Follow the steps
w1d1-3.text: Build 3 heads following the 4 steps: one from the front, one in three-quarter view, one in profile.

w1d1-3b.title: The head as a volume, Follow the steps
w1d1-3b.text: Build 3 heads following the 4 steps: one from the front, one in three-quarter view, one in profile.

w1d1-3c.title: The head as a volume, Follow the steps
w1d1-3c.text: Build 3 heads following the 4 steps: one from the front, one in three-quarter view, one in profile.

w1d1-4b.title: The head as a volume, Your turn
w1d1-4b.text: Here are finished faces, without their construction. Pick 2, find the sphere, side plane, axis and jaw under each one, then draw them.

w1d1-4c.title: The head as a volume, Your turn
w1d1-4c.text: Here are finished faces, without their construction. Pick 2, find the sphere, side plane, axis and jaw under each one, then draw them.

w1d1-5.title: The head as a volume, Challenge: a head in 1 minute
w1d1-5.text: Draw this head in 1 minute, construction included. Do it twice.

w1d2.title: The eyes
w1d2.text: Build a manga eye step by step, then put it on a face, from the front, in 3/4 and in profile.

w1d2-2.title: The eyes, Follow the steps
w1d2-2.text: Build 2 eyes following the 4 stages: a left eye and a right eye. The pointed corner always faces the outside of the face.

w1d2-3.title: The eyes, On the face
w1d2-3.text: A beautiful eye in the wrong place spoils the whole face. Four rules are enough to place it. The eye line: Halfway down the head, between the top of the skull and the chin. Lower, the character looks younger. The gap: The width of one eye between the two eyes. In 3/4 view: The far eye gets narrower and moves closer to the nose; the near one keeps its shape. In profile: You see only one eye, shaped like an arrowhead, and the iris becomes a thin oval.

w1d3.title: The nose
w1d3.text: A small wedge on the face: how to build it, and the 3 types of manga nose.

w1d3-1.title: The nose, Warm-up
w1d3-1.text: Draw 10 small triangles the size of a nose, turned every which way: it's the basic shape of the nose.

w1d3-2.title: The nose, The method
w1d3-2.text: Even when it's a single stroke, a manga nose is a volume: a small wedge on the face, of which you only draw a part. Where it goes: On the center line of the face, halfway between the eye line and the chin. The wedge: Sketch it lightly: a long triangle for the bridge, and a small flat underside where the nostrils are. One side only: Choose where the light comes from and ink only the shaded side, or only the underside. Erase the rest. When the head turns: In 3/4, the tip sticks out a little past the center line, toward the way the head turns. In profile, the nose comes out of the face outline as a small triangle.

w1d3-3b.title: The nose, Types of noses
w1d3-3b.text: The same wedge gives 3 different noses, depending on what you keep. Choose by the character's age and style. The dot: A dot or a tiny line under the tip. For cute characters and children. The triangle: The shaded side and the underside form a small triangle. For teens and adults. The drawn nose: The bridge, the tip and the nostrils. For realistic styles and older characters.

w1d3-3c.title: The nose, Types of noses
w1d3-3c.text: The same wedge gives 3 different noses, depending on what you keep. Choose by the character's age and style. The dot: A dot or a tiny line under the tip. For cute characters and children. The triangle: The shaded side and the underside form a small triangle. For teens and adults. The drawn nose: The bridge, the tip and the nostrils. For realistic styles and older characters.

w1d4.title: The mouth
w1d4.text: Build a manga mouth, closed or open, with its teeth and tongue, from every angle.

w1d4-1.title: The mouth, Warm-up
w1d4-1.text: Draw 10 little mouth lines, each with a different curve: straight, arched, wavy, lopsided.

w1d4-2.title: The mouth, The method
w1d4-2.text: In manga a mouth fits in 1 to 3 strokes. But those strokes follow the shape of the face. Where it goes: On the center line, closer to the nose than to the chin: a third of the way from one to the other. The line: A slightly curved stroke, narrower than the space between the eyes. Its corners set the mood. The lower lip: A short stroke under the line is enough to suggest the lip. No need to outline the lips. When the head turns: In 3/4, the far side of the mouth gets shorter. In profile, only a small notch remains under the nose, set back a little.

w1d4-3b.title: The mouth, Opening the mouth
w1d4-3b.text: An open mouth is the line opening into a shape, with what shows inside. Slightly open: A tiny oval or a small triangle in place of the line. Open: A D shape lying down: flat side at the top for a smile, rounder and taller for a shout. The teeth: A simple white band under the top of the mouth, without drawing each tooth. The tongue: A curve at the bottom of the open mouth: it fills the back and adds depth.

w1d5.title: Hair
w1d5.text: A mass around the skull, locks starting from the parting, and your character's head finally complete.

w1d5-1.title: Hair, Warm-up
w1d5-1.text: Draw 10 locks of hair in one stroke each: wide at the root, thin at the tip, curved like an S or a C.

w1d5-2.title: Hair, The method
w1d5-2.text: Hair isn't hundreds of lines: it's a volume sitting on the skull, cut into a few big locks. The hairline: It runs along the top of the forehead, a little below the top of the skull, and comes down in front of the ear: a C on the side plane, from the top of the eyes to the bottom of the nose. The mass: Hair has thickness: draw its overall shape around the skull, a little bigger than it, never stuck to it. The parting and the locks: Choose where the parting is: every lock starts from there. Cut the mass into big pointed locks. Locks follow the ball: In 3/4 and in profile, the locks wrap around the skull, like the construction lines of the head.

w1d5-3.title: Hair, Types of hairstyles
w1d5-3.text: Every hairstyle is built the same way. What changes is the shape of the mass and how the locks are drawn. Short and spiky: A round mass bristling with triangle locks pointing every way. Straight: Long, almost straight locks that fall under their own weight and split into points. Wavy or curly: S-shaped locks, or spirals gathered in clumps, never one by one. Tied up: Ponytail, pigtails, bun: draw the hair tie first, then the hair pulled toward it and the tuft coming out of it.

w1d5-4.text: Invent your character and draw their complete head from the front, in 3/4 and in profile: construction, eyes, nose, mouth, then their hairstyle. Long horizontal lines keep the eyes, nose and mouth at the same height on all 3.

head-1.title: Building the head in three steps: The skull
head-1.text: Start with a sphere or an egg shape.

head-2.title: Building the head in three steps: The side plane and the axis
head-2.text: Cut a flattened face on the side of the skull: that's the temple, where the ear will go. Then draw the vertical axis down the middle of the face: it curves as the head turns.

head-3.title: Building the head in three steps: The eye line and the jaw
head-3.text: Draw the eye line: it follows the surface of the face and turns with the head. Then connect the sides of the skull to the chin with simple lines.

head-rotation.title: Coach's exercise: the rotation
head-rotation.text: Imagine a small box inside the skull, as a guide to orient the head. Turn this guide, then place the features of the face on its surface.

w2.title: Expressions
w2.text: Build each emotion with the eyebrows, eyelids and mouth, control how strong it is, then push it the manga way.

w2d1.title: Joy
w2d1.text: Build a smile with 3 levers, eyebrows, eyelids and mouth, then its 4 shades.

w2d1-1.title: Joy, The method
w2d1-1.text: An emotion is always built in the same order: eyebrows, eyelids, mouth. Joy is all three going up. The eyebrows: Relaxed and slightly arched, a little raised. Never frowning. The eyelids: The rising cheeks push the lower lid up: the eye squints. In a big smile, it closes into an arc. The mouth: The corners go up. The stronger the joy, the more the mouth opens into a D, flat side on top. The cheeks: A small curve under the eye, or a few blush lines: the cheeks lift with the smile.

w2d1-2b.title: Joy, The 4 smiles
w2d1-2b.text: Joy has several levels: the same levers, pushed more or less. The soft smile: Closed mouth in a small curve, eyes open and calm. The big smile: Open mouth showing the upper teeth, squinting eyes. The laugh: Eyes closed in arcs, mouth wide open, head thrown back. The awkward smile: Small smile, eyebrows lifted in the middle, eyes looking away.

w2d2.title: Sadness
w2d2.text: Eyebrows lifting in the middle, eyes dropping, and 4 ways to be sad.

w2d2-1.title: Sadness, The method
w2d2-1.text: Same order, eyebrows, eyelids, mouth, but everything drops, except the middle of the eyebrows. The eyebrows: The inner ends go up, the outer ends go down: a slope like a tent. The eyelids: The upper lid drops over the iris, the gaze lowers. The eyes shine: add one more highlight. The mouth: The corners go down. Closed, it wobbles in a small wave; open, it turns square. The head drops: The eye line curves downward and the top of the skull shows more: the whole head says sadness.

w2d2-2b.title: Sadness, The 4 sadnesses
w2d2-2b.text: From a small letdown to sobbing, sadness builds in stages. The pout: Eyebrows barely lifted, lower lip pushed out a little. Teary eyes: A line of water on the lower lid and big trembling highlights. Tears: Drops running from the corner of the eye along the cheek. Sobbing: Eyes squeezed shut, mouth wide open and square, streams of tears.

w2d3.title: Anger
w2d3.text: V-shaped eyebrows, narrowing eyes, and anger from annoyance to fury.

w2d3-1.title: Anger, The method
w2d3-1.text: Still eyebrows, eyelids, mouth. Anger pulls everything toward the middle of the face. The eyebrows: The inner ends drop toward the nose: a V. Two small creases form between the brows. The eyelids: The upper lid comes down over the iris and straightens: the gaze hardens. Smaller pupils. The mouth: Closed, it tightens into a straight line or shows clenched teeth; open, it's a shout shaped like a trapezoid. Nose and cheeks: The top of the nose wrinkles and the cheeks tighten: a few lines are enough.

w2d3-2b.title: Anger, The 4 angers
w2d3-2b.text: Anger has its levels, and each one says something about the character. Annoyed: Eyebrows barely frowning, half-closed eyes, mouth twisted to the side. Sulking: V-shaped eyebrows, puffed cheeks, pressed lips, eyes to the side. Furious: Eyebrows very low, clenched teeth, creases on the nose. Shouting: Mouth wide open in a trapezoid, teeth showing, eyes wide.

w2d4.title: Surprise and fear
w2d4.text: Eyes opening wide: what separates a nice surprise from real fear.

w2d4-1.title: Surprise and fear, The method
w2d4-1.text: Eyebrows, eyelids, mouth: surprise and fear open everything. The difference is in the details. The eyebrows: Surprise: they go up high and stay rounded. Fear: they go up too, but lift in the middle. The eyelids: Wide open, with white all around the iris. In fear, the pupil becomes tiny. The mouth: Surprise: a relaxed open circle. Fear: the mouth stretches sideways and trembles. The head: In fear, the head sinks into the shoulders and pulls back; in surprise, it straightens up.

w2d4-2b.title: Surprise and fear, The 4 reactions
w2d4-2b.text: From astonishment to terror, four reactions to know. Astonished: Raised eyebrows, slightly bigger eyes, mouth in a small o. Shocked: Eyes wide open, small pupils, mouth dropping wide open. Worried: Eyebrows lifted in the middle, eyes darting to the side, pressed lips. Terrified: Tiny pupils, stretched trembling mouth, sweat on the forehead.

w2d5.title: Manga codes
w2d5.text: Sweat drops, veins, blushes, distorted eyes: manga's symbols, then your character's expression sheet.

w2d5-1.title: Manga codes, The method
w2d5-1.text: These symbols are a language every manga reader knows. They add to the expression, they don't replace it. The sweat drop: A big drop on the temple or behind the head: awkwardness, unease. The anger vein: A cross with curved branches on the forehead or temple: annoyance building up. The blush: Small slanted lines across the cheeks and nose: embarrassment, love, fever. Distorted eyes: Spirals for dizziness, hearts for love, stars for wonder.

w2d5-2.text: In funny scenes, manga goes further: the face gets simpler and stretches. Blank eyes: Two empty ovals, no iris: the character is in shock. w3.title: The body and its proportions
w3.text: Build a manga body with the right proportions, head to toe: torso, arms, legs, then the whole character.

w3d1.title: Proportions
w3d1.text: Measure a character with their own head, and the proportions by age and style.

w3d1-1.title: Proportions, The method
w3d1-1.text: To stop getting leg lengths wrong, measure your character with their own head, in 4 stages. The line and the head: Draw the character's height, then cut it into head heights, from the top of the skull to the chin. The landmarks: 2 heads: the chest. 3: the navel. 3.5: the crotch, the middle of the body. 5: the knees. 7: the feet. The widths: Shoulders about 2 heads wide, hips about 1.5 heads. The arms: With the arms down, the elbow falls at the waist and the fingertips at mid-thigh.

w3d1-2.title: Proportions, Ages and styles
w3d1-2.text: The number of heads changes with the character's age and the manga's style. Chibi: 2 to 3 heads: a huge head, a small round body. The child: 4 to 5 heads: big head, short legs, no defined waist. The teen: 6 to 7 heads: the most common in manga. The adult and the hero: 7.5 to 8 heads, up to 9 for an action hero: small head, long legs.

w3d2.title: The torso
w3d2.text: An egg rib cage, a box pelvis and the belly linking them: the center of the whole body.

w3d2-1.title: The torso, Warm-up
w3d2-1.text: Draw 10 eggs point down and 10 flat little boxes, from every angle.

w3d2-2.title: The torso, The method
w3d2-2.text: Before muscles and clothes, the torso is built with two volumes, in 4 stages. Neck and shoulders: A cylinder for the neck, then the shoulder line, a little below the chin. The rib cage: An egg, point down, from the shoulders to the bottom of the ribs, a little above the navel. The pelvis: A slightly flattened box, from the navel to the crotch. Belly and spine: Between rib cage and pelvis, a gap: the belly, which bends and twists. A curved line, the spine, links everything at the back.

w3d2-3.title: The torso, The 4 torsos
w3d2-3.text: With the same two volumes, you change the character's silhouette. Boy: Wide rib cage and square shoulders, narrow pelvis: a V. Girl: Smaller rib cage, slim waist, pelvis as wide as the shoulders: an hourglass. Slim: Narrow, elongated volumes, a thin neck. Heavy-set: A huge rib cage, a thick neck, shoulders rising almost to the ears.

w3d2-4.text: Here are dressed characters. For 2 of them, find the torso under the clothes: draw their rib cage and pelvis, then the outline.

w3d2-5.title: The torso, Challenge: side view
w3d2-5.text: Draw a torso in side view: the rib cage leans a little forward, the pelvis backward, and the back makes an S.

w3d3.title: The arms
w3d3.text: Two cylinders, three joints, and the positions of a bending arm.

w3d3-1.title: The arms, Warm-up
w3d3-1.text: Draw 10 quick cylinders, standing, lying down and tilted: two ellipses and two lines.

w3d3-2.title: The arms, The method
w3d3-2.text: An arm is built in 4 stages, from the shoulder to the hand, without worrying about muscles at first. The shoulder: A ball at the end of the shoulder line: the whole arm turns around it. Two cylinders: Upper arm and forearm have the same length; the upper one is thicker. Elbow and wrist: A small ball at the elbow, at waist level, a smaller one at the wrist. The hand stays a mitten for now. The outline: A round bump for the shoulder, then soft curves: never two parallel lines.

w3d3-3b.title: The arms, The 4 positions
w3d3-3b.text: The same cylinders, bent differently: four positions to know. Down by the side: Both cylinders aligned, the hand at mid-thigh. Bent: The elbow stays near the waist, the forearm rises: the cylinders overlap at the elbow. Raised: The shoulder rises with the arm: the shoulder ball lifts toward the ear. Crossed: The forearms pass in front of the torso: the front one hides part of the other.

w3d3-3c.title: The arms, The 4 positions
w3d3-3c.text: The same cylinders, bent differently: four positions to know. Down by the side: Both cylinders aligned, the hand at mid-thigh. Bent: The elbow stays near the waist, the forearm rises: the cylinders overlap at the elbow. Raised: The shoulder rises with the arm: the shoulder ball lifts toward the ear. Crossed: The forearms pass in front of the torso: the front one hides part of the other.

w3d3-4.title: The arms, Your turn
w3d3-4.text: Here are arms in varied positions. Redraw 3 of them: shoulder, cylinders and joints first, then the outline.

w3d3-5.title: The arms, Challenge: arms crossed
w3d3-5.text: Draw a character standing with arms crossed over the chest, from the front: which arm goes in front, which behind?

w3d4.title: Legs and feet
w3d4.text: Thigh, knee, calf, then foot: legs that really carry the character.

w3d4-1.title: Legs and feet, Warm-up
w3d4-1.text: Draw 10 simple feet as long triangles, in profile then from the front.

w3d4-2.title: Legs and feet, The method
w3d4-2.text: A leg is built in 4 stages, from the hip down to the foot. The hip: A ball on each side of the pelvis: the legs start there, not from the bottom of the pelvis. Thigh and knee: The thigh is the biggest cylinder in the body. The knee falls halfway between hip and foot. The calf: It bulges at the back of the leg, then thins down to the ankle. The foot: A long triangle, almost as long as the head. The ankle bone sits higher on the inside than on the outside.

w3d4-3.title: Legs and feet, The 4 positions
w3d4-3.text: Standing, walking, sitting, kneeling: the legs change everything. Standing: The legs angle slightly inward: the feet come together under the body. Walking: One leg in front, one behind: the back knee bends and the heel lifts. Sitting: The thighs go horizontal and the knees come up to hip level. Kneeling: The knee touches the ground, the back foot bends on its toes.

w3d4-5.text: Draw a character sitting on a chair in profile: back, thighs and shins make three lines at almost right angles.

w3d5.title: Your character, full body
w3d5.text: The whole body put together, front and side view, with your character's silhouette.

w3d5-1.title: Your character, full body, Warm-up
w3d5-1.text: Draw 3 standing stick figures in 10 seconds each, landmarks included.

w3d5-2.title: Your character, full body, The method
w3d5-2.text: To put a whole body together, always follow this order, from measuring to outline. The lines: Draw the landmarks across the whole page: top of the head, chin, chest, navel, crotch, knees, feet. The stick figure: A spine, the shoulder line, the hip line, then the limbs down to the landmarks. The volumes: Rib cage, pelvis, arm and leg cylinders, placed on the stick figure. Outline and clothes: An outline in soft curves, then a T-shirt and pants following the volumes.

w3d5-3.title: Your character, full body, The 4 silhouettes
w3d5-3.text: Before drawing your character, choose their silhouette: it says who they are before their face does. The triangle: Wide shoulders, narrow hips: a strong character, a hero. The hourglass: Shoulders and hips of the same width, slim waist: elegant, graceful. The rectangle: Everything the same width: a simple, sporty or still childlike character. The round: The belly wider than everything else: a gentle, funny or greedy character.

The round: The belly wider than everything else: a gentle, funny or greedy character.

w3d5-4.text: Draw your character full body, front and side view side by side: the lines, the stick figure, the volumes with their silhouette, then the outline and simple clothes.

limbs-1.title: Exercises for each part: Arms
limbs-1.text: Draw an upper arm and a forearm in ten orientations, then bend the elbow at different angles. Careful: the elbow, the wrist and the shoulder aren't interchangeable and don't connect the same way.

limbs-2.title: Exercises for each part: Legs
limbs-2.text: Build the thigh, the lower leg and the foot. Practice with sitting, standing, crouching and moving poses.

limbs-3.title: Exercises for each part: Hands
limbs-3.text: Start with a box for the palm. Add the fingers as simplified segments, respecting their length and direction. Work on open hands first, then fists, and finally more complex gestures.

limbs-4.title: Exercises for each part: Feet
limbs-4.text: Build a wedge-shaped volume before adding the toes. Check the heel, the sole and the orientation of the ankle.

w4.title: Poses
w4.text: Get your character moving: a line of action, weight that sits right, a twist, depth, and poses that tell something.

w4d1.title: The line of action
w4d1.text: One curve through the whole body, and 4 lines for 4 energies.

w4d1-1.title: The line of action, Warm-up
w4d1-1.text: Draw 10 curves in one stroke each, top to bottom: Cs and Ss, more and more curved.

w4d1-2.title: The line of action, The method
w4d1-2.text: A well-built mannequin can still look stiff. To make it move, start with a line, even before the head. The curve: A single line from the head to the foot carrying the weight. The stick figure: The spine follows the line; the shoulders and hips cross it. The mannequin: Rib cage and pelvis sit on the curve, the limbs carry it to the end. The outline: Go over the pose without breaking the curve: the back and the supporting leg follow it.

w4d1-3.title: The line of action, The 4 lines
w4d1-3.text: The shape of the line sets the energy of the pose. The C: One curve: the character pushes, pulls or leans. The S: Two curves: a walk, an elegant pose, a relaxed body. The I: Almost straight: a calm character, or one stretched with their whole body, as in a jump straight up. The big arc: A very arched C: action, a strike, momentum.

w4d1-3b.title: The line of action, The 4 lines
w4d1-3b.text: The shape of the line sets the energy of the pose. The C: One curve: the character pushes, pulls or leans. The S: Two curves: a walk, an elegant pose, a relaxed body. The I: Almost straight: a calm character, or one stretched with their whole body, as in a jump straight up. The big arc: A very arched C: action, a strike, momentum.

w4d1-4.text: Pick 3 poses from the sheet. For each one, draw its line of action first, then build its mannequin on it.

w4d1-5.title: The line of action, Challenge: 30 seconds
w4d1-5.text: Draw 4 poses in 30 seconds each, from photos or people around you: only the line of action.

w4d4.title: Foreshortening
w4d4.text: The arm coming at you, the leg going away: drawing depth.

w4d4-1.title: Foreshortening, Warm-up
w4d4-1.text: Draw 6 cylinders seen more and more from the end: the last one is just a circle.

w4d4-2.title: Foreshortening, The method
w4d4-2.text: A limb coming toward you is built in 4 stages, with cylinders. The direction: Draw the limb's axis: it's very short, since it points at you. The ellipses: The ends of the cylinders become almost circles: rounder as they face you. Near is big: A hand reaching at you can be as big as the head: enlarge what's in front. The overlap: The front cylinder hides the start of the one behind: draw it first.

w4d4-3.title: Foreshortening, The 4 foreshortenings
w4d4-3.text: Four situations where depth changes everything. Arm reaching at you: A huge hand, the arm almost hidden behind it. Leg coming forward: A kick at you: the sole gets bigger than the torso. Seen from above: Big head and shoulders, tiny feet at the bottom. Seen from below: Huge feet and legs, a tiny head at the top.

w4d4-4.title: Foreshortening, Challenge: the punch
w4d4-4.text: Draw a character throwing a punch straight at you: the fist bigger than their head.

w4d5.title: Action poses
w4d5.text: Running, jumping, striking: the right moment pushed all the way, then your character in 3 poses that tell a story.

w4d5-1.title: Action poses, Warm-up
w4d5-1.text: Draw 6 lines of action in 5 seconds each: a run, a jump, a punch, a fall...

w4d5-2.title: Action poses, The method
w4d5-2.text: An action pose is built in 4 stages and pushes everything to the max. The key moment: Not the middle of the move: the instant just before (arm pulled back) or just after (the punch flying). The pushed line: Push the line of action further than is possible: manga loves it. The diagonal: Lean the whole pose on a diagonal: it looks in motion, where a vertical pose looks still. The silhouette: Fill your pose in black: the action must still read. Keep the arms and legs away from the body.

w4d5-3.title: Action poses, The 4 actions
w4d5-3.text: Four actions found in every manga. Running: Body leaning forward, one arm and the opposite leg in front, one foot in the air. Jumping: The body stretched like a bow, legs tucked or stretched behind. The punch: The striking arm and its shoulder go forward, the other arm pulls back for balance. The kick: The supporting leg bends, the chest leans away from the kicking leg.

w4d5-4.title: Action poses, Your character in 3 poses
w4d5-4.text: Draw your character in 3 poses telling a little story: before (getting ready), during (jumping or striking), after (landing or getting up). Draw the 3 lines of action side by side first, then the mannequins, the outline and the face.

dynamic-1.title: Four tools to bring your poses to life: The line of action
dynamic-1.text: Before any detail, draw a curve that expresses the overall movement. It keeps poses from being too straight and symmetrical.

dynamic-2.title: Four tools to bring your poses to life: Opposing axes
dynamic-2.text: Tilt the shoulders and the pelvis differently to create a natural movement. They shouldn't both be horizontal all the time.

dynamic-3.title: Four tools to bring your poses to life: Foreshortening
dynamic-3.text: An arm pointing at the viewer looks shorter because it goes into depth. Build it with the axis and the volumes rather than trusting its apparent length.

dynamic-4.title: Four tools to bring your poses to life: Balance
dynamic-4.text: Watch where the weight of the body sits and where it touches the ground. A pose must look like it can hold, or clearly show why the character is falling or jumping.

torso-1.title: Essential exercise: turn the torso and the pelvis independently: Neutral pose
torso-1.text: Stack the torso and the pelvis without any real twist. Check their relative sizes and the general axis of the body.

torso-3.title: Essential exercise: turn the torso and the pelvis independently: Tilt
torso-3.text: Lean both volumes, then adapt the spine and the shoulders. Watch how the center of gravity moves.

w5.title: Hands and clothes
w5.text: Finish your character: hands that make gestures, clothes that fold and hang in the right places, an outfit that tells who they are.

w5d1.title: The hand in blocks
w5d1.text: A box palm, cylinder fingers: the most dreaded part becomes simple.

w5d1-1.title: The hand in blocks, Warm-up
w5d1-1.text: Put your hand on the table and draw its overall shape in 30 seconds, without a single detail.

w5d1-2.title: The hand in blocks, The method
w5d1-2.text: A hand is only a box and cylinders. It's built in 4 stages. The palm: A flat box, a little longer than it is wide. The whole hand nearly covers the face. The fingers: Three small cylinders each, shorter and shorter. The knuckles form an arc, and the middle finger is the longest. The thumb: It starts at the bottom of the palm, on the side, with a big pad at its base. It folds toward the palm, not like the fingers. The outline: Round off the cylinders, add a crease at each joint and simple nails. No more.

w5d1-3b.title: The hand in blocks, The 4 views
w5d1-3b.text: The same hand changes completely depending on where you look from. The palm: Palm creases, the thumb pad, fingers narrowing at the tips. The back: Knuckles in an arc, nails, flatter fingers. From the side: The palm becomes a thin box, the fingers hide behind one another. Fingertips first: The fingers point at you: very short little cylinders, almost circles.

Fingertips first: The fingers point at you: very short little cylinders, almost circles.

w5d1-5.text: Draw your own hand with the fingers spread wide, then with the fingers together. 1 minute each, in blocks.

w5d3.title: Folds
w5d3.text: Clothes fold where the body bends or pulls: find those points and the folds come by themselves.

w5d3-1.title: Folds, Warm-up
w5d3-1.text: Draw 3 cylinders and wrap them in spiral folds, like a rolled-up sleeve.

w5d3-2.title: Folds, The method
w5d3-2.text: A fold is never random. It's drawn in 4 stages, starting from the body. The body underneath: Draw the arm, the leg or the torso in volumes: the fabric will rest on it. Pull points: Find where the fabric pulls: shoulder, elbow, knee, waist. Mark them with a small circle. The fabric outline: The garment follows the body without sticking to it, tighter near the pull points. The folds: Draw the folds from the pull points, in strokes that taper at the end.

w5d3-3.title: Folds, The 4 folds
w5d3-3.text: Depending on how the fabric is held, it makes 4 kinds of folds. The star: Lines radiating from a pull point: the armpit, the crotch. The zigzag: In the crook of a bent elbow or knee, the fabric piles up in a zigzag. The spiral: Around a turning arm or leg, the folds wrap around. The diamond: Between two pulling points, the fabric hollows into diamonds: a bending back, an outstretched arm.

w5d3-4c.text: Redraw these 3 folding garments. For each one, find the pull point first, then the type of fold.

w5d3-5.title: Folds, Challenge: arms up
w5d3-5.text: Draw a character stretching with both arms up: the T-shirt rides up and the folds start from the armpits.

w5d4.title: Hanging fabric
w5d4.text: Skirts, capes, wide sleeves, scarves: fabric that hangs and flies in the wind.

w5d4-1.title: Hanging fabric, Warm-up
w5d4-1.text: Draw 10 quick waves at the bottom of a bell shape: it's the hem of a skirt.

w5d4-2.title: Hanging fabric, The method
w5d4-2.text: Hanging fabric is built in 4 stages, from where it hangs down to its edge. The hanging point: The waist for a skirt, the shoulders for a cape: everything hangs from there. The overall shape: A bell or a rectangle hanging down, wider at the bottom than at the top. The tubes: The fabric falls in vertical tubes starting from the hanging point. The hem: The edge makes a wave: each tube bulges forward there, then tucks back.

w5d4-3.title: Hanging fabric, The 4 fabrics
w5d4-3.text: The same principle for four garments that move. The skirt: Pleated: regular tubes; full: big waves. The cape: It falls from the shoulders down the back and hides part of the body. The wide sleeve: It hangs under the raised arm, like a small curtain. The wind: In the wind, fabric flies away from the movement and unrolls in wider and wider waves.

w5d4-4.title: Hanging fabric, Your turn
w5d4-4.text: Draw 2 seated characters: one in a long skirt, the other in a long coat. The fabric falls from the knees to the floor in tubes.

w5d4-4b.title: Hanging fabric, Your turn
w5d4-4b.text: Draw 2 seated characters: one in a long skirt, the other in a long coat. The fabric falls from the knees to the floor in tubes.

w5d4-5.title: Hanging fabric, Challenge: in the wind
w5d4-5.text: Draw a character standing in the wind: their cape, their scarf and their hair all fly the same way.

w5d5.title: Your character's outfit
w5d5.text: An outfit that tells who they are, then your complete character, in their signature pose.

w5d5-1.title: Your character's outfit, Warm-up
w5d5-1.text: Draw 5 collars around a cylinder neck: crew neck, shirt, hood, sailor collar, turtleneck.

w5d5-2.title: Your character's outfit, The method
w5d5-2.text: An outfit is drawn in layers, over the body, in 4 stages. Body first: Draw the whole mannequin, even under a long coat: it's what carries the outfit. Thickness: Fabric rests on the body without sticking to it: leave a small gap, bigger for thick fabric. The edges: Collars, hems, belts and cuffs wrap around the body: draw them as curves, never as straight lines. A detail that tells: One or two details say who they are: a badge, a scarf, gloves, a cape.

w5d5-3.title: Your character's outfit, The 4 outfits
w5d5-3.text: Four basic manga outfits, each with its own rules. School uniform: Blazer or sailor collar, pleated skirt or straight trousers: clean, symmetrical lines. Sportswear: Soft, close-fitting fabrics, lots of small folds at the joints. Everyday clothes: Hoodie, jeans, sneakers: thick fabrics, wide folds, layers. Adventure gear: Coat, cape, belts, boots: layers and accessories that tell of the journey.
